solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One in gorgeous hat moving around island

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit within it, so one letter goes among the others
letters that are moving around shift position, so the whole set is rearranged

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sports a splendid hat that keeps moving about on their head.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter I joins the eleven letters of 'gorgeous hat' and the twelve are rearranged into SOUTH GEORGIA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a remote British territory in the South Atlantic, a mountainous landmass surrounded by sea.

clue.text: Men on horse held up music producer

indicators.note: in a down entry, something held up is lifted to read bottom to top

blocks.note: OR, other ranks, are the ordinary soldiers
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Soldiers on horseback hold up a record producer, like a hijacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the soldiers above the horse in the down entry; 'held up' reads as a robbery but turns the horse over.
explanation.definitionFit: A church organ is an instrument, something that produces music from pipes and keys.

clue.text: Might I grab your lime and cut it?

definitions.text: Might I grab your lime and cut it?

blocks.clueFragment: Might I grab your lime and cut it?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone asks to take your citrus fruit and slice it, as for a drink
setter's reading: a lime is also the linden tree, and this professional prunes trees by cutting off limbs

explanation.surface: A bartender asks politely to take your lime and slice it for your gin.
explanation.walkthrough: Lime the fruit gives way to lime the linden tree, and 'cut' becomes the work of someone who operates on trees.
explanation.definitionFit: An arborist who prunes or fells trees, offering to lop a linden in your garden.

clue.text: Mongrel dog ran around earl and whined

indicators.note: a mongrel is of mixed breed, so these letters are mixed up
to go around something is to surround it, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: A mutt ran circles round a nobleman and howled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mongrel' looks like an adjective describing the dog, but it signals the mixing of the letters of 'dog ran' with E.
explanation.definitionFit: To groan and to whine are both to complain with a low, plaintive sound.

clue.text: Not even funny

blocks.note: first meaning: of a number, not divisible by two
second meaning: strange, peculiar

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as 'not even slightly amusing'; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes numbers like three or seven, and also anything strange or peculiar.

clue.text: Pat dogs or different creature

indicators.note: making something different changes its form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Stroke the dogs, or some other animal if you prefer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is very general; the wordplay does all the work here.
explanation.definitionFit: A gastropod, such as a snail or slug, is a kind of mollusc and so a living animal.

clue.text: Decoration-wise, one has tree up inside at Xmas!

definitions.text: Decoration-wise, one has tree up inside at Xmas!

blocks.note: surface reading: an odd, almost rude image of something with a tree stuck up inside it
setter's reading: the figure placed on top of a Christmas tree sits with the tree's tip pushed up inside its skirt

explanation.surface: A cheeky festive remark about a decoration with a tree pushed up inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The traditional tree-topper is a winged figure whose hollow robe slips over the top branch, so the tree really is up inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A winged heavenly figure is the classic ornament fixed at the very top of a Christmas tree.

clue.text: Car half-made by mostly rubbish robots

indicators.note: only half of the word is wanted, so the rest is cut away
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: auto is short for automobile
the first half of the word
tat is rubbish, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A car only half built by robots that are mostly junk.
explanation.walkthrough: TAT is British slang for cheap, shoddy goods. The surface pictures a factory line, but every word is a piece of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Automata is the plural of automaton, a self-operating machine, which is what a robot is.

clue.text: Bit of elastic attached to a jumper?

definitions.text: Bit of elastic attached to a jumper?

blocks.clueFragment: Bit of elastic attached to a jumper?
blocks.note: surface reading: a stretchy strip sewn onto a sweater, a jumper being a British word for a pullover
setter's reading: the jumper is a person leaping from a height, held by a stretchy line tied to the ankles

explanation.surface: Someone stitches a strip of elastic onto a woolly pullover.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a jumper is a sweater, which is the false picture; the person who jumps off a bridge on a rope is the real one.
explanation.definitionFit: The elastic rope that saves a leaper from a bridge or crane is the thing clipped to them.

clue.text: Talk about a lengthy series of events

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to gas is to chatter idly
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone chats on about a long, drawn-out chain of happenings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talk about' looks like a single verb phrase, but 'about' acts on the talk alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long story or a protracted affair, the kind of drawn-out tale that never ends.

clue.text: Medals hung around one lad for actions

indicators.note: something hung around another thing encircles it, as a medal ribbon circles a neck

blocks.note: gong is British slang for a medal or award; the setter's plural is loose
the Roman numeral for one
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: Decorations were hung on a young man in recognition of his deeds.
explanation.walkthrough: A gong is British slang for a medal. The medal surrounds I, and the lad follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Goings-on are happenings or activities, usually suspicious ones, so things people do and get up to.

clue.text: Exclude pilot one’s regularly seen in pub

blocks.note: to bar is to shut out
to fly a plane is to pilot it

explanation.surface: A pilot who is always in the pub ought to be grounded.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase at the end; the verbs at the start are both pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A barfly is a habitual drinker who hangs about bars, a fixture at the counter most nights.

clue.text: National labs heading into distribution

indicators.note: being put into distribution spreads things about, so the letters are scattered and reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A national laboratory chain is moving into product distribution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National' reads as an adjective about the labs, but it is a noun: a citizen of a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A national is a citizen of a particular state; here a citizen of Bangladesh.

clue.text: Large as well as light

blocks.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
and means as well as

explanation.surface: Something can be big and yet weigh very little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like the opposite of large, but it is a verb: to come down and settle.
explanation.definitionFit: To light upon something is to alight or come to rest on it, as a bird or aircraft touches down.

clue.text: Barperson caught in act is questioned

indicators.note: something caught in another is trapped inside it

blocks.note: a brief is British slang for a barrister, a lawyer called to the bar
a deed is an act

explanation.surface: A bartender caught red-handed is interrogated by police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barperson' suggests someone pulling pints, but the bar is the legal profession; a brief is slang for a barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: To debrief someone is to question them closely after a mission or event.

clue.text: Foreign article about one apt to shoot swimmer

indicators.note: to face about is to turn round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: der is a German word for 'the'
a snapper is a photographer, someone who shoots pictures

explanation.surface: A foreign newspaper story about a gunman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' suggests a gun, but here it means taking photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: The red snapper is a sea fish, and a fish is something that swims.

clue.text: Head of school entertained by schoolboy language

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, and only that is put inside
a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: its first letter
an Etonian is a pupil at Eton, the English public school

explanation.surface: A headmaster is amused by the slang his pupils use.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is a famous English boarding school for boys; an Etonian is one of its pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonian is the Finnic tongue spoken in Estonia, so a language.

clue.text: Toy bible a lord manufactured

indicators.note: something manufactured is made up from parts, so these letters are assembled anew

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman has produced a toy version of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the first word; everything else is fodder and its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This famous fashion figure made by Mattel is a plaything for children.

clue.text: Old people procuring line for high priests?

definitions.note: a definition by example, hence the question mark

indicators.note: to procure is to get hold of, so one piece takes in another

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
races are peoples
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Elderly people gather a line of dialogue meant for senior clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' looks like one phrase, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece, priests and priestesses at shrines like Delphi delivered divine prophecies, so a broadly fair, question-marked example.

clue.text: Slightly contrary information

indicators.note: contrary means going the opposite way, so the letters run back to front

blocks.note: a tad means slightly

explanation.surface: A fact that is a little at odds with what we thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slightly contrary' reads as one description of the information, but it is a phrase of two words written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Data are facts and figures collected for analysis, the raw material of knowledge.

clue.text: Give out a wave, perhaps, using radio

indicators.note: on radio we only hear words, so the spelling is judged by the ear

blocks.note: a sine curve is one kind of wave, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Someone hands out a greeting over the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A wave' suggests a hand gesture, but it is a sine wave from maths and physics.
explanation.definitionFit: To assign tasks or seats is to allot or distribute them to people.

clue.text: Completely pack up belongings

blocks.note: first meaning: to fill something tightly to the top
second meaning: one's things or possessions

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like moving house; the two halves are a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to cram something full; as a noun it covers a person's things and possessions.

clue.text: Former royal a cold-hearted bandit shot

definitions.note: a noun phrase for one who gives up a throne

indicators.note: to have something at heart is to hold it in the middle
something shot is wrecked or ruined, so its letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the tap abbreviation for cold
taken as written

explanation.surface: A callous outlaw gunned down a one-time member of the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like the bandit's fate, but it scrambles the bandit with C at its heart.
explanation.definitionFit: An abdicant is someone who renounces a throne, so a monarch who no longer reigns.

clue.text: Try fun class A drug hit: lose it, gag and snap

blocks.note: an attempt or go at something
good times in company, the Irish craic
a smokable form of cocaine
a sharp blow
to break down under pressure
a joke or quip
to break with a sharp sound

explanation.surface: Someone tries a hard drug for fun, loses control, gags and finally snaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Every one of the seven words or phrases is a separate meaning of the same five-letter word, a multiple definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an attempt, a fracture, a joke, a blow, a drug and a breakdown in different senses.

clue.text: Attractive and tan Polish expert

blocks.note: slang for physically fit and good-looking
a pale yellowish-brown colour
to shine or rub a surface
an enthusiast who knows a subject well

explanation.surface: A handsome, suntanned man from Poland who knows his stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' wants to be the nationality, its capital hiding the verb meaning to shine; all four words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means muscular and good-looking, a light brown shade, to burnish, and a knowledgeable enthusiast.

clue.text: Cook a lamb with ease, adding new salt

indicators.note: to cook is also to fiddle or doctor something, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A simple recipe: roast lamb without fuss, seasoned with fresh salt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' looks like seasoning for the lamb, but an old salt is an experienced sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt is a seasoned sailor, and an able seaman is a rank of trained sailor in the navy.

clue.text: Unopened post creates trouble

indicators.note: something unopened has not had its front broken into, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: mail, which is post, minus its first letter

explanation.surface: Leaving your letters unopened only causes problems.
explanation.walkthrough: MAIL is the British word for post; dropping its opening letter leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ail is to afflict or bother, as in 'what ails you?', so to trouble someone.

clue.text: Cobblers found in Bow and Sweden

blocks.note: a fiddlestick is a violin bow
S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: Shoemakers can be found in Bow, the East London district, and in Sweden.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow looks like the London place name, but it is the stick used to play a violin. Cobblers is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive British exclamations meaning nonsense or rubbish, used to reject a claim.
